newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says 1998 budget tough, but on schedule.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says 1998 budget tough, but on schedule.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday planning for the 1998 budget was proving tough, but he would come up with a package with a federal deficit of 58 billion marks.
Waigel, in remarks prepared for delivery to the so-called finance planning council, said the economic environment for drawing up the budget was "extremely difficult".

Growth was too slow to cut high German unemployment in 1998 or help tax revenues, and the government had to contend with an extra burden of 30 billion marks revealed by the latest tax revenue forecasts published last months, he said.

Waigel's remarks to the council, which groups finance officials from state and local governments and a Bundesbank representative, did not refer directly to Bonn's efforts to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
But, sketching his strategy, Waigel said the government would seek to press forward with reforms to the tax system and exhaust all possible savings and consolidation possibilities.

Waigel said that coalition negotiations on state finances both this year and next were on schedule and constructive, with broad agreement on the need to accelerate privatisation, cut the solidarity income tax surcharge next year, and tighten up on departmental spending.
Waigel also said that the government would hold to its budget planning schedule, which envisages cabinet approval on July 11.
